title: Pre-meeting brief: Stripe

tldr.text: Stripe launched US stablecoin payouts (USDC/OUSD) to crypto wallets in 160+ markets across nine blockchains, positioning as a lower-cost alternative to SWIFT.
Stripe unveiled Stripe Pay, a B2B payments product that mirrors the P2P experience to extend its reach across business payments.
Stripe advanced its AI strategy with the Metronome and OpenRouter acquisitions, while its Tempo blockchain gains traction for remittances, cross-border payouts, and agentic commerce.

Within that limit, the agent can check out without asking again. New York was excluded from the initial rollout. A Privy noncustodial wallet holds the balance. Link enforces the customer's spending rules, and Stripe Issuing supplies a virtual debit card for checkout. The merchant receives a card payment without integrating crypto. Link's terms specify USDC for the noncustodial agent-wallet balance, despite OUSD being the default elsewhere in Stripe's stablecoin offering. Link’s terms generally make the user responsible for those purchasing decisions, while treating payment-execution errors separately and preserving applicable rights. Stripe also offers protections for qualifying agent purchases, initially through Muse. sources.snippet:
The October announcement placed Global Payouts alongside Treasury and Issuing in a shared financial services offering. Stripe said the products can share customer verification information and work with Open Standard’s OUSD stablecoin and the Tempo blockchain.

## USDC payouts support nine blockchain networks

The supported USDC networks are Arbitrum, Avalanche C-Chain, Base, Ethereum, Optimism, Polygon, Solana, Stellar and Tempo. OUSD payouts are available on Base, Ethereum, Solana and Tempo.

Before sending funds, Stripe instructs businesses to check that the recipient’s wallet supports both the selected stablecoin and the chosen network. [...] At the time, Stripe said businesses could send instant stablecoin payouts to recipients in 160 markets and traditional currency payouts to more than 100 markets directly through its Dashboard.

The announcement described hosted forms and APIs for fintech companies that want to build payouts into their own products. Named uses included loan disbursements, remittances, investment withdrawals and neobank cash-outs.

The rise of embedded finance has led businesses to expect payments to fit seamlessly into the platforms and workflows they already use. Yet business-to-business payments often remain time-consuming and costly. Stripe is looking to simplify the process with a service that resembles the consumer peer-to-peer payment experience. Businesses could search for a vendor’s profile and transfer funds via the Stripe Pay plug-in. For companies that lack a recipient’s full payment details, Stripe also offers a business directory. “Stripe is trying to make paying another business as easy as sending money to a handle,” said Brian Riley, Director of Credit at Javelin Strategy & Research. “Businesses can identify recipients through their Stripe profiles instead of entering traditional bank details. The real headline may be ‘free’ not ‘instant,’ as Stripe Pay is advertising these business-to-business transfers with no transfer fee.” Providing Clarity and Control Several trends are driving demand for better B2B payment solutions. The growth of vertical software-as-a-service platforms has given businesses of all sizes access to industry-specific tools, with seamless payment acceptance central to the model. Meanwhile, the consumer payments experience has raised expectations for B2B transactions to be digital-first and easy to use. Beyond convenience, payment efficiency has implications for cash flow and working capital. This is one reason virtual cards have gained traction. They give organizations greater control over payment timing and more visibility into spending and liquidity. Whether Stripe Pay can deliver similar advantages will depend on how businesses use the service and how it integrates with their existing payment processes.
